paragraphs: ChemCoTBench addresses a gap between answering chemistry questions from remembered knowledge and reasoning through changes to molecular structures. The paper argues that existing evaluations emphasize retrieval, while tasks such as improving a molecule’s properties or predicting a reaction require a sequence of chemically meaningful decisions. Its contribution is a framework that makes those decisions explicit and assessable.

The framework represents molecular transformations through modular operations such as addition, deletion, and substitution. These operations provide a vocabulary for breaking a chemical problem into smaller steps, with molecular structure and chemical constraints grounding the reasoning. The arithmetic analogy concerns how solutions are organized: each operation contributes to a transparent workflow that can be examined step by step.

The authors evaluate models on Molecular Property Optimization and Chemical Reaction Prediction. They also introduce ChemCoTDataset, containing 22,000 examples with expert-annotated reasoning chains for fine-tuning. Together, the benchmark, dataset, reasoning taxonomy, and baseline evaluations provide infrastructure for studying systematic chemical reasoning. The stated contribution is a foundation for training and evaluation, rather than a reported breakthrough in a particular chemical discovery.
neurips-2025-beyond-chemical-qa-evaluati.tldr: ChemCoTBench evaluates chemical reasoning through explicit molecular operations and supplies 22,000 expert-annotated examples for training.

paragraphs: CAPE adapts transformer positional encoding to features that have causal relationships but no natural sequence. Conventional positional encodings require an ordering of the inputs. For non-sequential data, the paper instead seeks a representation of how features relate causally, so attention can use information beyond an assigned position in a list.

The method first uses generalized structural equation modeling to identify a weighted directed acyclic graph over the features. It then embeds that graph in hyperbolic space using a hyperboloid-based construction designed to preserve causal strength and causal specificity. These geometric representations become positional encodings, which are converted into rotary form for use within the transformer’s self-attention mechanism.

The theoretical analysis establishes three properties of the resulting encodings: attenuation associated with causal distance, attenuation associated with causal generality, and robustness to positional disturbances. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets empirically support these properties and the method’s effectiveness for non-sequential features. The contribution connects an identified causal graph to attention through geometry, giving the transformer a structured account of feature relationships.
neurips-2025-causality-induced-positiona.tldr: CAPE converts causal graphs over unordered features into geometric positional encodings for transformer attention.

paragraphs: Drag-and-Drop LLMs tackles the repeated training cost of adapting a language model to new tasks. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA reduce the number of parameters that need updating, but still require a separate optimization run for each downstream dataset. DnD instead learns to generate the adaptation parameters directly from a small batch of unlabeled task prompts.

A lightweight text encoder compresses the prompts into conditioning embeddings. A cascaded hyper-convolutional decoder then turns those embeddings into the complete set of LoRA matrices. The parameter generator itself is trained on a diverse collection of prompt-checkpoint pairs. Once that training is complete, it can produce task-specific updates in seconds without a new optimization run for each task.

The reported results include up to 12,000-fold lower overhead than full fine-tuning and average performance gains of up to 30% over the strongest training LoRAs on unseen benchmarks. The authors also report a 40% cross-domain performance improvement without target data or labels. These findings support prompt-conditioned weight generation as an empirical alternative for rapidly specializing language models.
neurips-2025-drag-and-drop-llms-zero-sho.tldr: DnD learns to turn unlabeled task prompts into LoRA weights, enabling rapid adaptation without per-task optimization.

paragraphs: EnzyControl focuses on generating enzyme backbones with control over both their intended function and the substrate they act on. The paper identifies limitations in available binding data and in existing models’ ability to condition new enzyme structures on particular substrates. It addresses these issues through a curated dataset and an adaptation method for a pretrained protein generation model.

The dataset, EnzyBind, contains 11,100 experimentally validated enzyme-substrate pairs curated from PDBbind. EnzyControl conditions generation on substrates and catalytic sites annotated through multiple sequence alignment, extracted automatically from the curated data. Its central component, EnzyAdapter, is a lightweight module that adds substrate awareness to a pretrained motif-scaffolding model. A two-stage training process further refines the generated structures.

On EnzyBind and EnzyBench, the authors report the best performance across the evaluated structural and functional metrics. They highlight improvements of 13% in designability and 13% in catalytic efficiency relative to baseline models. These results support combining catalytic-site information with substrate conditioning to guide backbone generation toward structures that better satisfy the evaluated design objectives.
neurips-2025-enzycontrol-adding-function.tldr: EnzyControl adds substrate and catalytic-site conditioning to enzyme backbone generation, supported by a curated enzyme-substrate dataset.

paragraphs: The John ellipsoid is the largest-volume ellipsoid that fits inside a convex body. This paper develops faster ways to approximate it for a particular class of bodies: centrally symmetric polytopes described by linear inequalities of the form −1 ≤ Ax ≤ 1. The matrix A has n rows, d columns, and full column rank, defining the setting for the algorithms.

The first algorithm uses sketching and has running time approximately proportional to the number of nonzero entries in A plus d raised to the matrix multiplication exponent, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This connects much of the computation to the amount of matrix data actually present. The second algorithm uses the treewidth of A’s dual graph and runs in roughly n times the square of that treewidth, again suppressing logarithmic factors.

The previous stated running time scales as n times d squared. The new bounds therefore expose benefits from sparsity and graph structure in this optimization problem. Both algorithms approximate the ellipsoid, and their guarantees concern the specified symmetric polytopes rather than arbitrary convex-body representations.
neurips-2025-faster-algorithms-for-struc.tldr: Two algorithms accelerate John ellipsoid approximation by exploiting matrix sparsity or the treewidth of an associated graph.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to fine-tune discrete diffusion models using reward signals. These models have attracted interest for generating complex discrete structures, including language, but applying policy-gradient methods to them remains challenging. The objective is to make reward-based adaptation practical for this model family, extending a style of optimization commonly used in reinforcement learning from human feedback.

The proposed algorithm is Score Entropy Policy Optimization, or SEPO. It is designed to optimize non-differentiable rewards: feedback can evaluate a generated result without providing a derivative that can be passed directly through the reward calculation. The authors present SEPO as an efficient, broadly applicable policy-gradient algorithm with theoretical justification for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models.

Numerical experiments across several discrete generation tasks demonstrate the method’s scalability and efficiency. The contribution therefore combines an optimization algorithm, a theoretical basis, and empirical evidence across multiple tasks. Its significance is in making discrete diffusion models more amenable to reward-driven fine-tuning, so their adaptation can be guided by evaluations of generated outputs.
neurips-2025-fine-tuning-discrete-diffus.tldr: SEPO provides a theoretically justified policy-gradient method for fine-tuning discrete diffusion models with non-differentiable rewards.

paragraphs: FLOWING addresses morphing between images or shapes, where corresponding features must move into alignment while appearance changes smoothly over time. Neural representations based on multilayer perceptrons offer differentiable, mesh-free deformation models. However, the paper identifies costly regularization, unstable training, and poor feature alignment as obstacles when standard networks are used to produce coherent morphing sequences.

The proposed framework represents warping through a differential vector flow. It encodes structural properties of that flow directly into the network architecture, ensuring continuity, invertibility, and coherence over time. This design makes the transformation’s structure part of the representation itself, reducing dependence on costly regularization to obtain a well-behaved deformation.

The framework supports morphing of both two-dimensional images and three-dimensional shapes. Experiments include face and image morphing as well as Gaussian Splatting morphing, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art quality and faster convergence. These findings support the value of designing neural deformation architectures around flow properties: the same structural choices underpin both stable transformations and effective feature alignment.
neurips-2025-flowing-implicit-neural-flo.tldr: FLOWING builds structural flow properties into neural architectures to produce coherent image and shape morphing with faster convergence.

paragraphs: ForgerySleuth applies multimodal language models to detecting image manipulation. The paper identifies a problem with using these models directly: their explanations can contain hallucinations and excessive reasoning. Its approach combines analysis of manipulation clues with an explicit spatial output, so the system can indicate which parts of an image it judges to have been tampered with.

The model fuses multiple clues and produces a segmentation marking manipulated regions. To support this task, the authors construct ForgeryAnalysis using a Chain-of-Clues prompt. The dataset includes analysis and reasoning text, adding explanatory supervision to image manipulation detection. A separate data engine builds a larger dataset for the pretraining phase.

The experiments demonstrate the usefulness of ForgeryAnalysis and report that ForgerySleuth significantly surpasses existing methods in generalization, robustness, and explainability. The contribution brings together training data, clue-based analysis, and region-level detection. Its stated findings suggest that this combination can make multimodal models more effective at both locating image edits and explaining the evidence behind their assessments.
neurips-2025-forgerysleuth-empowering-mu.tldr: ForgerySleuth combines manipulation-clue reasoning with region segmentation and dedicated training data to improve image forgery detection.

paragraphs: Adaptive Cognition Policy Optimization, or ACPO, addresses reasoning models that generate unnecessarily long reasoning even when a task does not require it. Inspired by dual-process theory, the framework trains models to allocate effort according to difficulty and switch between thinking modes. The goal is efficient reasoning that adjusts to the problem being solved.

ACPO introduces special reasoning tokens that explicitly identify thinking modes in the generated reasoning path. During reinforcement learning, it combines online estimates of task difficulty with a token-length budget to guide mode switching and reasoning. These signals connect the model’s choice of thinking mode to both the challenge of the task and the amount of reasoning it produces.

Training proceeds in two stages. Supervised fine-tuning first teaches the model to generate reasoning paths with explicit mode labels; ACPO then improves adaptive switching through reinforcement learning. Experiments show reduced redundant reasoning and cognitive allocation that responds to task complexity. The reported result is an efficient hybrid reasoning approach, with the mode-selection behavior made explicit in its outputs.
neurips-2025-incentivizing-dual-process-.tldr: ACPO trains reasoning models to switch thinking modes according to task difficulty and token budgets, reducing redundant reasoning.

paragraphs: Simple Energy Adaptation, or SEA, studies alignment with human feedback while a language model is answering a query. Existing approaches generate several complete responses and use a reward model to search among them. The paper identifies a weakness in this strategy: a weak base policy or a small candidate pool can leave the search with few informative options.

SEA instead adapts responses through gradient-based sampling in a continuous latent space. It formulates inference as repeated optimization of an energy function over continuous actions, with that function defined by the optimal policy. This gives the procedure a way to move an initial response toward a better one rather than relying entirely on selection among separately sampled responses.

The authors report relative improvements of up to 77.51% on AdvBench and 16.36% on MATH over the second-best baseline. These are benchmark-specific empirical results, supporting the effectiveness of continuous-space adaptation in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is a different search formulation for inference-time alignment, using iterative refinement to address the limitations of a finite response pool.
neurips-2025-inference-time-alignment-in.tldr: SEA aligns responses at inference time by refining continuous latent representations with gradient-based sampling.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes what a transformer can represent from whether an efficient algorithm can learn it from data. Earlier expressivity results showed that transformers can simulate sophisticated computations. Here, the authors establish polynomial-time learnability results for single-layer transformers with linear attention, specifically in the strong, agnostic PAC learning framework.

The main reduction turns learning optimal multi-head linear attention into finding an optimal kernel predictor in a suitably constructed reproducing kernel Hilbert space. That reformulation provides the route to efficient learning. The authors also develop a polynomial-time procedure that checks whether every best-fitting multi-head linear attention network for a given dataset performs the same computation.

This agreement test offers a strong notion relevant to out-of-distribution generalization: it asks whether the best-fitting networks are computationally identical, beyond merely matching the observed data. Experiments examine learning random linear attention networks, key-value associations, and finite-automaton execution. Together, the results connect learnability, computational agreement, and empirical behavior for the specified single-layer linear-attention model class.
neurips-2025-learning-linear-attention-i.tldr: The paper proves polynomial-time learning results for single-layer linear-attention transformers and gives an efficient test for agreement among best-fitting networks.

paragraphs: metaTextGrad addresses an extra layer of design in language-model optimization. Frameworks such as DSPy and TextGrad use language models to improve prompts, demonstrations, predictions, or other system components. Yet the optimizers that make those improvements are generally designed by people and intended to work across many tasks, leaving their own design choices outside the optimization process.

The paper proposes a meta-optimizer that improves an existing optimizer for a particular task. It combines two components: a meta prompt optimizer and a meta structure optimizer. Together, these target both the prompts used by the optimizer and its structure, making the optimization procedure itself something that can be adapted to the task.

Across multiple benchmarks, the combined approach significantly improves performance, with average absolute gains of up to 6% over the best baseline. These findings support treating the optimizer as another adaptable component of an AI system. The practical significance is that a general-purpose language-model optimizer can be further tailored, rather than assuming its initial human-designed configuration is the best fit for each task.
neurips-2025-metatextgrad-automatically-.tldr: metaTextGrad improves language-model optimizers themselves by adapting their prompts and structure to specific tasks.

paragraphs: Multimodal Negative Learning addresses situations where a strong input modality dominates learning and weaker modalities struggle to contribute. Conventional approaches can encourage weaker modalities to imitate the dominant one’s target-class predictions. The paper argues that this alignment risks suppressing information that is distinctive to the weaker modality.

The proposed framework changes the guidance signal. Dominant modalities dynamically guide a weaker modality to suppress non-target classes, rather than directly pushing its target-class prediction toward their own. This negative-learning strategy is intended to stabilize the decision space while retaining information specific to each modality. The authors derive the framework from a robustness perspective and introduce a dynamic guidance mechanism suited to this objective.

The theoretical result tightens a lower bound on multimodal robustness by increasing the Unimodal Confidence Margin. The method also reduces empirical error for weak modalities, particularly in noisy and imbalanced settings. Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness and generalizability against competing approaches. The findings connect a change in cross-modal supervision with both a formal robustness bound and improved observed learning behavior.
neurips-2025-multimodal-negative-learnin.tldr: Multimodal Negative Learning helps weaker modalities by teaching them which classes to suppress while preserving their distinct information.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a policy from an existing dataset when the objective is average reward over an infinite horizon. The setting permits large or infinite state spaces. The proposed actor-critic algorithm uses a linear function class to estimate values and adopts pessimistic reward estimates, making conservative evaluation central to policy optimization from offline data.

Its critic computes both an estimate of the current policy’s average reward and the associated policy gradient by solving a fixed-point Bellman equation. This avoids the successive regression problems used in finite-horizon settings. The resulting computation can be expressed as a second-order cone program, giving the critic a computationally tractable optimization formulation.

The learning guarantee depends on a weak partial data coverage condition: the offline data must align well with the expected feature vector of a comparator policy. Under that condition, the authors establish optimal sample complexity proportional to ε⁻² for obtaining a near-optimal policy, up to model misspecification errors. Both the coverage condition and the approximation error qualification are part of the stated guarantee.
neurips-2025-offline-actor-critic-for-av.tldr: A pessimistic offline actor-critic algorithm achieves optimal average-reward sample complexity under a partial coverage assumption, up to model misspecification.

paragraphs: Optimize Any Topology, or OAT, aims to make structural topology optimization fast across varied design specifications. The task seeks material layouts with minimum compliance under specified constraints. The paper identifies fixed square grids, narrow sets of boundary conditions, and post-hoc optimization as restrictions of existing deep-learning approaches, limiting their flexibility for engineering design.

OAT combines an autoencoder that accommodates different shapes and resolutions, an implicit neural-field decoder, and a conditional latent-diffusion model. It is trained on OpenTO, a new dataset containing 2.2 million optimized structures and 2 million distinct boundary-condition configurations. The framework directly predicts layouts conditioned on aspect ratio, resolution, volume fraction, loads, and fixtures.

Evaluation covers four public benchmarks and two challenging unseen tests. The authors report reductions in mean compliance of up to 90% relative to the best prior models, with inference below one second on a single GPU. Tested resolutions range from 64 × 64 to 256 × 256, with aspect ratios reaching 10:1. These results support fast, flexible prediction across the evaluated structural design settings.
neurips-2025-optimize-any-topology-a-fou.tldr: OAT predicts structural layouts across varied shapes, resolutions, and constraints, reporting fast inference and lower compliance on evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: PRIMT uses foundation models to support preference-based reinforcement learning for robot behavior. This learning approach avoids manually engineering rewards, but can require extensive human feedback. It also faces ambiguous comparisons and difficulty assigning credit to the parts of a behavior that deserve reward. PRIMT addresses these issues through synthetic feedback and generated trajectories.

For feedback, the framework combines vision-language models and language models through hierarchical neuro-symbolic fusion. This uses their complementary evaluations of robot behavior to produce more comprehensive judgments. Foresight trajectory generation supplies initial examples to the trajectory buffer, helping reduce ambiguity early in learning when useful comparisons may be difficult to obtain.

PRIMT also augments trajectories in hindsight for counterfactual reasoning, using a causal auxiliary loss to improve credit assignment. This component focuses reward learning on how alternative behavior relates to outcomes. Across two locomotion tasks and six manipulation tasks on various benchmarks, the framework outperforms foundation-model-based and scripted baselines. The results support combining multimodal evaluation with trajectory synthesis to improve preference-based robot learning.
neurips-2025-primt-preference-based-rein.tldr: PRIMT combines multimodal synthetic preferences with generated and counterfactual trajectories to improve robot reward learning.

paragraphs: Labyrinth is a benchmark environment for measuring how well imitation-learning agents generalize beyond their training conditions. The paper identifies a problem with existing benchmarks: training and evaluation may differ too little to provide a meaningful test. Labyrinth makes those differences controllable, allowing researchers to establish that training, evaluation, and test settings are genuinely distinct.

Researchers can vary the environment’s structure, starting positions, goals, and task complexity. Its discrete, fully observable state space and known optimal actions support detailed interpretation of agent behavior. These properties make it possible to examine particular sources of generalization difficulty instead of relying only on performance across a loosely defined collection of tasks.

The environment also offers variants involving partial observability, keys and doors, and ice-floor hazards. Those variants expand the kinds of challenges that can be tested within the same benchmarking framework. The contribution is controlled, reproducible evaluation infrastructure: it provides a way to ask more precise questions about where imitation-learning agents succeed or fail when conditions change, supporting the development of more robust agents.
neurips-2025-quantifying-generalisation-.tldr: Labyrinth makes imitation-learning generalization measurable through controlled changes to environments, goals, starting points, and task complexity.

paragraphs: Diffusion Chain of Lateral Thought, or DCoLT, treats the intermediate stages of diffusion text generation as reasoning actions. Reinforcement learning rewards the correctness of the final answer and optimizes the whole trajectory leading to it. Intermediate states can involve bidirectional, nonlinear changes and need not form grammatically correct sentences, allowing reasoning to follow the model’s diffusion process.

The authors implement this idea in two diffusion language models. For SEDD, a continuous-time discrete diffusion model, its concrete score defines a probabilistic policy over intermediate steps. For the masked diffusion model LLaDA, the method learns how to order token prediction and unmasking through a ranking-based Unmasking Policy Module using the Plackett-Luce model.

Experiments on mathematics and code generation use public data and 16 H800 GPUs. The reinforced models outperform compared diffusion models trained with supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or both. For LLaDA, the authors report reasoning accuracy increases of 9.8%, 5.7%, 11.4%, and 19.5% on GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval, respectively. The findings highlight both diffusion-trajectory optimization and token-unmasking order as useful components of reasoning training.
neurips-2025-reinforcing-the-diffusion-c.tldr: DCoLT improves diffusion-model reasoning by rewarding final-answer correctness and optimizing intermediate generation steps, including token-unmasking order.

paragraphs: SafeVLA studies how to incorporate explicit safety constraints into vision-language-action models used as robot policies. These models can support general-purpose behavior, but deployment introduces risks to people, the robot, and its surroundings. The paper proposes an integrated safety approach that connects the specification of safety requirements with training and targeted evaluation.

The approach first models safety requirements and actively elicits diverse unsafe behaviors. It then uses safe reinforcement learning to constrain the policy and evaluates the resulting behavior against targeted risks. A constrained Markov decision process supplies the formal framework, while a min-max optimization perspective trains the policy against the safety risks that have been elicited.

On long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks, the authors report an 83.58% reduction in cumulative safety-violation cost relative to the state-of-the-art comparison, alongside a 3.85% increase in task success rate. They also report mitigation of long-tail risks and extreme failure scenarios, plus generalization of safety behavior under out-of-distribution perturbations. These findings support the evaluated safety-performance trade-off rather than establishing unrestricted safety in every deployment.
neurips-2025-safevla-towards-safety-alig.tldr: SafeVLA combines explicit safety modeling, risk elicitation, and constrained reinforcement learning to reduce robot safety violations while maintaining task performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a post-training method that converts large pretrained flow-matching diffusion models into samplers requiring only a few steps. Existing shortcut models support skipping along generation trajectories, but depend on specialized step-size embeddings. Adding those embeddings to standard pretrained models would require retraining from scratch at a cost approaching pretraining.

The proposed method avoids that requirement through velocity-field self-distillation. It trains in the space of velocity fields rather than sample outputs and learns online from self-guided distillation. This allows standard models such as Flux to acquire more aggressive shortcuts without a step-size embedding. The authors give a concrete efficiency example: producing a three-step Flux model in less than one A100 GPU-day.

The method can also be incorporated into pretraining so that models learn efficient few-step flows from the outset, with the authors reporting no compromise in quality. They further demonstrate few-shot distillation using, for example, ten text-image pairs for diffusion models with around a dozen billion parameters. The reported state-of-the-art performance supports a substantially cheaper route to few-step generation in these settings.
neurips-2025-shortcutting-pre-trained-fl.tldr: Velocity-field self-distillation turns pretrained flow-matching models into few-step samplers without requiring specialized step-size embeddings.

paragraphs: SPICED addresses continual EEG decoding as new individuals arrive with different signal characteristics. The challenge is to adapt to this variation while retaining useful knowledge from earlier learning. Inspired by synaptic homeostasis, the framework balances strengthening important memories with weakening others, aiming to preserve both stable knowledge and the capacity to keep learning.

Its dynamically expanding synaptic network uses three mechanisms. Critical memory reactivation selects task-relevant memories. Synaptic consolidation strengthens those memories and increases their priority for replay during later adaptation. Periodic synaptic renormalization weakens memory traces globally to preserve learning capacity. Together, these processes regulate which past information most strongly influences ongoing learning.

The framework preferentially replays task-discriminative memories associated with newly encountered individuals, while suppressing replay priority for detrimental memories. The authors report robust adaptation and reduced catastrophic forgetting during long-term continual learning, with effectiveness validated on three EEG datasets. The contribution applies a biological regulation principle to an unsupervised continual-learning system, making selective memory reinforcement and replay central to adaptation.
neurips-2025-spiced-a-synaptic-homeostas.tldr: SPICED uses biologically inspired memory strengthening, weakening, and replay to support continual EEG adaptation while reducing forgetting.

paragraphs: SpiderSolver is a transformer designed to solve partial differential equations on domains with complicated shapes and irregularly distributed points. The paper addresses the difficulty of extending transformer-based PDE methods to such geometries. Its central idea is to organize the spatial representation around the domain boundary, making geometry part of how the model groups and processes its inputs.

The method divides the domain into spiderweb-like patches guided by boundary geometry. These patches become tokens for a coarse attention mechanism that captures interactions across the whole domain. A separate fine attention mechanism refines interactions between the boundary and nearby interior points. The two levels combine global spatial relationships with detailed treatment of the boundary region.

Evaluation spans seven datasets, including cars, airfoils, and blood flow in the human thoracic aorta, together with cases involving Navier-Stokes, Darcy flow, elasticity, and plasticity equations. The authors report state-of-the-art performance across the evaluated datasets and metrics, as well as better out-of-distribution generalization. These findings support geometry-aware tokenization and multiscale attention for the tested PDE problems.
neurips-2025-spidersolver-a-geometry-awa.tldr: SpiderSolver uses boundary-guided spatial patches and two levels of attention to solve PDEs on complex geometries.

paragraphs: SplitFlow addresses text-guided image editing with rectified flow models. The paper identifies inaccurate inversion and entangled editing gradients as reasons that edited images may fail to reflect a target prompt. Its framework uses an inversion-free formulation and reorganizes the editing flow around separate semantic parts of the requested change.

The method splits the target prompt into sub-prompts, computes a separate flow for each, and combines them into a single editing trajectory. The authors empirically observe that this decomposition increases diversity in the target space. However, they also find that semantic alignment still requires consistent guidance from the full target prompt, so decomposition alone is insufficient for the desired editing behavior.

To balance those effects, SplitFlow uses projection and soft aggregation inspired by gradient-conflict resolution in multi-task learning. It adaptively weights the sub-target velocity fields, suppressing redundant semantic directions while emphasizing distinct ones. Experiments show improvements over existing zero-shot editing methods in semantic fidelity and attribute disentanglement. The findings support coordinated flow decomposition as a way to preserve diverse edits while keeping them consistent with the overall instruction.
neurips-2025-splitflow-flow-decompositio.tldr: SplitFlow combines flows for semantic sub-prompts with full-prompt guidance to improve inversion-free image editing.

paragraphs: Shape and Style Guidance, or SSG, improves training-free test-time adaptation for vision-language models. Existing methods commonly use prediction entropy to select visual features and update a cache of test examples. The paper argues that this overlooks factors that may generalize better, particularly sensitivity to shape and insensitivity to style.

SSG applies shape and style corruptions to each test image, then measures how predictions change relative to the original image. This perturbed prediction difference becomes a signal for reweighting high-confidence visual features and their predictions. The intended effect is to emphasize features whose behavior reflects the desired shape-sensitive and style-insensitive properties during adaptation.

The cache update combines the perturbation measure with entropy, aiming to retain samples with high entropy and generalizable factors. This adds information about responses to image changes to the criteria used for storing examples. Across out-of-distribution and cross-domain benchmarks, the authors report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods and promising computational efficiency. The results support perturbation-guided adaptation without an optimization stage at test time.
neurips-2025-training-free-test-time-ada.tldr: SSG uses prediction changes under shape and style corruptions to guide training-free adaptation of vision-language models.

paragraphs: VETA-DiT targets the memory and computation costs of diffusion transformers through post-training quantization. Converting weights and activations to low-bit representations can make inference more efficient, but the paper identifies severe generation-quality degradation when this is applied to diffusion transformers. Its framework addresses both differences across channels and changes across denoising steps.

First, the method analyzes quantization error through inter-channel variance and uses a Karhunen–Loève Transform enhanced alignment to equalize that variance. This prepares the representation for quantization at low bit widths. Second, a temporally adaptive calibration method identifies denoising timesteps that are especially difficult to quantize, accounting for activation distributions that change during the iterative generation process.

Experiments cover image and video generation using W4A4, meaning four-bit weights and four-bit activations. The authors report acceptable visual quality under this aggressive configuration. Relative to the baseline, FID decreases by 33.65 for DiT-XL/2 and 45.76 for PixArt-Σ. These results support treating channel variation and timestep variation as separate sources of error when designing low-bit diffusion-transformer quantization.
neurips-2025-veta-dit-variance-equalized.tldr: VETA-DiT improves four-bit diffusion-transformer quantization by equalizing channel variance and adapting calibration across denoising timesteps.
